_note: How an answer in English is compared (see sl.json for the fields). same: a contraction is the same answer as its long form (don't = do not, I'm = I am, it's = it is, can't = cannot; he's got = he has got: 's before got is has, so it comes first; Jack's at home = Jack is at home, only before a word a possessive never stands before: an article, not, a preposition of place, here, there, a possessive, always, never, very; I'd like = I would like); a number from 21 to 99 with or without its hyphen (twenty-one, twenty one), an ordinal too (twenty-first, twenty first); a hundred and five as the American a hundred five; the American spelling as the British (color = colour, favorite = favourite, center = centre, meter = metre, gray = grey, mom = mum, traveling = travelling, pajamas = pyjamas, plow = plough, math = maths, dialog = dialogue, program = programme), and -ize and -ise both British (realise, realize). No letters to fold. ending_letters: a word's ending is its last letter, also over five letters (Slovene's two), so a slip one letter before it is a slip (usualy for usually, walkd for walked) while the -s, -d and -g themselves stay the ending (walk for walks, sittin for sitting). loose: a contraction typed without its apostrophe is almost, with the apostrophe hint, never right (cant, isnt, dont, wont, Im, youre, theyve, hes got, whats, theres for can't, isn't, don't, won't, I'm, you're, they've, he's got, what's, there's), as phone keyboards hide it; words of their own stay out (its, were, well, ill, id, lets, hell, shell, wed, shed), so its for it's and were for we're stay wrong. wrong: the plural's known mistakes, each only for a noun of its group, never a slip of the keyboard on another noun: -s for -es after x, z, ch, sh, ss (boxs for boxes, churchs for churches, glasss for glasses) and buss for buses; potatos, tomatos for potatoes, tomatoes; -fes for -ves on the nouns that make it (knifes, wifes, lifes, calfes for knives, wives, lives, calves; gloves and loves keep their slips); woman for women and women for woman (one letter apart, else forgiven as a slip; man and men are too short for one); the numbers' spelling mistakes (fourty for forty, forteen for fourteen, ninty for ninety, ninteen for nineteen, for for four), which a slip in the stem would forgive; the -ing form's spelling, each only for a verb of its rule: the consonant not doubled (siting, runing, swiming, hoping for sitting, running, swimming, hopping), the silent e kept (makeing, comeing, writeing for making, coming, writing) and a consonant doubled where it isn't (writting, comming); the ordinals' (nineth for ninth, eigth for eighth, twelth for twelfth, fith and fivth for fifth, twentyth for twentieth, fourtieth for fortieth); were and where, each for the other (one letter apart, else forgiven as a slip); than and then, each for the other (one letter apart: German's als is never then); the comparative's, the superlative's and the adverb's spelling, each only for a word of its rule: the consonant not doubled (biger, hoter, thinest for bigger, hotter, thinnest), -y kept before an ending (happyer, easyest, happyly for happier, easiest, happily), -ful + -ly with one l (carefuly for carefully; usualy stays a slip); those for these and these for those (one letter apart: near or far, a real mistake); the present simple's -es after o and -ies after a consonant (gos, dos for goes, does; flyes, carryes, studyes, and a plural's babyes, for flies, carries, studies, babies).
_nonstandard_note: nonstandard: what people say that writing doesn't want: almost, the standard form shown, one way only (good for well, never well for good). A double negative only after a negative in its sentence, so Is there nothing to eat? stays wrong for anything. Not a worksheet item's spoken, which is right: COURSE.md, Spoken forms.
